Our work begins with a question: how can we provide earlier warning of agricultural nematode threats? Through surveys, dialogue, education, and collaboration, we connect our project with the situations in which it might be used. Explore our work through the four pathways below.

blocks.text: Starting with a hidden agricultural threat

blocks.body: Plant-parasitic nematodes live in soil and roots, but symptoms above ground do not always reveal their cause. When crops turn yellow, wilt, or grow poorly, growers must distinguish water stress, nutrient problems, and pests or diseases. They also need to know when testing can still inform management. These practical questions motivated our project on early warning of agricultural nematode threats.

Our project explores engineered yeast that responds to nematode-associated ascaroside signals and produces a visible output. Human Practices connects this concept with agricultural production, diagnostic expertise, public understanding, and potential use. We explain our project to others and bring their questions back into team discussions.

blocks.text: Bringing different experiences into the project

blocks.body: Farm visits helped us understand where testing might fit into agricultural routines. Plant protection specialists and academic experts challenged us to consider detection timing, representative samples, and the assumptions behind our approach. Exchanges with universities and other iGEM teams provided opportunities to compare experimental designs and research routes. Our questionnaire explored public understanding of nematodes and testing, while teaching and outreach introduced underground disease and synthetic biology to wider audiences.

We also collected soil samples, prepared sampling guidance, and discussed the resources needed for continued work with industry contacts and sponsors. Together, these activities addressed a shared question: if a test is to move beyond the laboratory, whose needs should it address, in what settings, and with what information?

Our work produced a questionnaire and statistical notes, interview records, sampling guidance, age-adapted lesson plans, and outreach materials. These resources support our own research and offer practical examples for other teams: deriving survey questions from project questions, retaining field context alongside samples, and documenting teaching and feedback across partnerships. Relevant materials are presented in the resource sections of each page.
